assumptions: same keys as EXP-C18-02 (avalanche, seed 1802) and EXP-C18-03 (key sets, seed 1803)
throughput (batch of 16384 keys of 64 bytes, median of 3, shared machine) is stored under timings only
falsification: H-C18-7: more than 256 (resp. 256^p) distinct values. H-C18-8: any flag for QC-LS, QC-ISO or QC-NIMINV. H-C18-9: QC-ARP with BIC max < 0.5.
hypothesis: H-C18-7: for the reverse-pass hash, keys sharing their first 7 bytes receive at most 256 distinct hash values; for the p-pass forward hash, keys sharing the last 7 message bytes receive at most 256^p values (Theorem 6, checked on data). H-C18-8 (bold): the cascade QC (8 passes, final state output, 8 zero bytes of finalisation) over the random Latin square, the group isotope and the nimber inversion quasigroup has avalanche at the BLAKE2b noise floor, |z| <= 3 and collision ratio within 2% on all four key sets, and no full 64-bit collisions. H-C18-9: the cascade over x + c(y) (ARP) still fails bit independence.
methodology: (a) For 50 random 7-byte prefixes, hash 4096 keys with that prefix (random 9-byte suffixes) with QG-LS p2+rev and count distinct values; for 50 random 7-byte suffixes do the same with the forward 1-pass hash (bound 256). (b) Avalanche, bit independence, chi-square and collisions for the four cascades, exactly as in EXP-C18-02/03.
question: EXP-C18-03 showed massive collisions of the tail-output hashes on structured keys. Does the tail-information bound (Theorem 6) account for them exactly, and does a cascade whose output is the final state of 8 parallel passes behave like the good baselines?

summary: tail bound: reverse-pass hash takes 256-256 distinct values on 4096 keys sharing a 7-byte prefix; forward 1-pass hash 256-256 on keys sharing the last 7 message bytes (bound 256)
